Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette: Forty years ago, Mateo had found himself pressed against a concrete wall in a windowless room, his wrists bound in coarse wire that dug deeper with every futile pull. There had been no exit, no gap to slip through, only the heavy silence and the sudden, sharp reports of firearms firing in the adjacent corridor. He remembered the dry heat of the space, the dust coating his tongue, and the way his mind had quietly lifted away from the blows, sliding into a thick, numb distance so he would not have to feel them. When the men finally left, he told himself it was his own fault, that if he had kept his posture lower, if he had chosen his words differently, none of it would have happened. He carried that certainty with him when he returned to the United States, settling in a quiet neighborhood where he could work with his hands and stay beneath any notice. Over the decades, the welding bay became his routine, but also a space that constantly echoed the old room. The booth was tightly enclosed, his heavy gloves and thick visor narrowing his vision until he was certain he could never predict who might step through the entrance or what might come next. He learned to watch the alley through the narrow gap in his protective gear, his shoulders permanently drawn tight. When a backfire cracked outside or a heavy service door slammed, his breath would catch and his body would brace as if the wire were still on his wrists again. In the shop hours, he moved with the same careful deference. When the foreman raised his voice or questioned a weld, Mateo would immediately agree, nodding and offering extra care. At home, widowed for a decade, he avoided pressing any topic, never letting frustration surface, because he was sure that showing any edge would draw the wrong kind of attention. When the memories of that room rose, he forced his thoughts toward the hum of the transformer or the rhythm of his own breathing, detaching from the images before they could settle, telling himself firmly that they were only old noise. Yet the past did not stay buried. When he tried to explain the ordeal to his daughter, the words fractured in his mouth. He would start with the room, the silence, the cold concrete, but then his voice would stall, the thread snapping, leaving only a tight chest and a heat that rushed up his neck. He realized he felt it again before he even named it-the same weight on his shoulders, the same metallic taste in his mouth, as though the floor beneath him had not changed at all. And when he finally let himself remember the full arc of it, a dark fury would ignite in his stomach, a rage so sharp it made his hands tremble. He blamed himself for not fighting harder, for the silence he had kept when others were hurt, for the choices he thought had sealed his fate. He was certain that danger could appear anywhere, from anyone, and that the only way to endure it was to stay invisible, to keep his thoughts locked away, to never give the past a foothold in the present. Now at seventy, Mateo found his routines fraying. The last two months had brought a new urgency: a pressure gauge on an old compressor had burst with a report that sounded exactly like a rifle shot, and he had frozen in the corner of his garage, unable to move until the echo faded. The shop foreman had noticed his withdrawal, leaving work piling up in the corner because Mateo could no longer bear the sound of metal dropping or the feeling of his boots pinned beneath a fallen crate. He had come to the clinic because his hands no longer trusted him with the torch, because he could not sleep without pacing the hallway, and because he was tired of carrying the weight of a room that had long since been emptied out. He wanted to understand why his body still braced for a door that would not open, what he could do to stop the anger from burning through his chest when the memories returned, and how he might finally forgive himself for surviving it all.
